note: Shows frontier reasoning models collapse completely past a complexity threshold, the strongest evidence yet against vendor reasoning claims.
title: The Illusion of Thinking: Understanding the Strengths and Limitations of Reasoning Models via the Lens of Problem Complexity

reading.body:
Frontier reasoning models show complete performance collapse past a complexity threshold, with no graceful degradation, suggesting their reasoning claims rest on narrower capabilities than vendors disclose.

The study tested reasoning models across puzzles of varying difficulty using controlled environments that isolate problem complexity. On medium-difficulty tasks, these models outperformed standard language models. On harder problems, both model types failed entirely, but reasoning models stopped allocating their available computational budget to the attempt. This is not a smooth decline in accuracy. It is a cliff edge where the claimed thinking process simply ceases to function.

The practical implication is narrow. A reasoning model that performs well on benchmark-style tasks at medium difficulty will not scale to genuinely hard problems through additional compute or inference time. Organizations evaluating these models for high-stakes decision support or complex analysis need to test on problem classes matching their actual requirements, not assume vendor benchmarks predict performance on novel hard problems. The models do not degrade gracefully under load. They stop working.

This reveals a fundamental architectural limitation rather than a training or data issue. Reasoning models fail at exact computation and algorithmic reasoning, not merely at novel questions. The boundary between domains where reasoning improves performance and domains where it fails appears fixed by how these systems are built. Whether additional buildings and power devoted to reasoning model development can move that boundary remains unanswered by this data.

explain_beginner: Newer AI models are sold as being able to think before they answer, showing their reasoning step by step, and companies claim this makes them much better at hard problems. This paper, from Apple researchers, tested that claim directly using classic logic puzzles, like the Tower of Hanoi, where you can precisely dial the difficulty up or down by changing the puzzle's size. The result, at easy difficulty, the plain, non thinking models actually did fine, sometimes better. At medium difficulty, the thinking models pulled ahead as advertised. But past a certain difficulty, every model, thinking or not, collapsed to near zero accuracy. Strangest of all, the thinking models did not even try harder as problems got more difficult, they visibly used less reasoning effort right when the puzzles got hardest, despite having plenty of room left to keep working. A later paper disputed some of the specific test conditions used here.
explain_business: The practical warning for anyone buying or building on reasoning branded AI models is that vendor benchmarks showing strong performance on moderate difficulty tasks may not predict what happens on your hardest real cases, since this paper found a sharp collapse in accuracy past a specific complexity threshold rather than a gradual decline. For a company deploying reasoning models on complex analysis, planning, or multi step decision tasks, the finding implies testing at the actual difficulty ceiling of your use case, not just typical cases, before trusting model output in production, since the failure mode here is a hard collapse, not a graceful one. That said, this finding is actively disputed by other researchers who argue the test setup itself, not the models, caused some failures, so treat this as one data point suggesting caution around task complexity rather than a settled ceiling, current as of mid-2025 model generations and likely to keep shifting.
explain_practitioner: Shojaee and colleagues at Apple evaluate large reasoning models against standard LLMs using controllable puzzle environments that let them dial problem complexity precisely while keeping logical structure constant, then analyze both final answers and internal reasoning traces token by token. They report three complexity regimes, at low complexity, standard LLMs match or beat reasoning models, at medium complexity, reasoning models show a genuine advantage from extra thinking tokens, and at high complexity, both model types collapse to near zero accuracy. The counterintuitive finding is that reasoning effort, measured in tokens spent, rises with complexity only up to a point, then declines even though the model has not hit its token budget limit, and the authors also report the models fail to reliably execute exact algorithms and reason inconsistently across structurally similar puzzles. A follow up paper argued some of these apparent failures actually reflected output length constraints and puzzle representation choices rather than a genuine reasoning ceiling, a live methodological dispute practitioners should treat as unresolved rather than final.
